data.turoyo: Qayəm u darwiš, azze, maʕazle, maḥšamle w daməx bu kon d Ḥetəm Aṭṭay.
data.translation: Da stand der Derwisch auf und ging mit; Ḥêtim-eṭ-ṭai erwies ihm Ehre und bewirtete ihn; darauf legte sich der Derwisch in Ḥêtim's Zelt zum Schlafe nieder.

rationale: Thin Preterit cell: honour and feeding in a hospitality scene; the host switch is contextual, not a rule inferred from translation.

data.turoyo: Mətyaqalle lu Saʕid, omər: "Duš əzzan l gabayna, gmaʕaznox." — komalle u Saʕid.
data.translation: Said glaubte es ihm und sagte: "Komm, lass uns zu mir gehen, ich will dich bewirten." Schon wollte er ihn mit sich nehmen,

rationale: Thin Infectum cell: prospective hosting with second-person guest suffix.

data.turoyo: Azze u kurrəko su Saʕid, maʕazle lu Saʕid hol ʕaṣriye.
data.translation: Der Jüngling aber ging mit Said nach Hause, und dieser bewirtete ihn bis zum Abend.

rationale: Thin Preterit cell: hosting until evening distinguishes actual entertainment from mere invitation.

data.turoyo: Deri yawmo maʕəzle lu kurrəko u Saʕid.

rationale: Thin Preterit cell: l-marked boy as host and zero-marked Said as guest; roles reverse from the preceding day.

Inherited maʕəzlox already has bewirten, and PrS 7/10 juxtaposes maʕazle with feeding; PrS 83/47–48 describes reciprocal hospitality extending until evening. Widen the existing gloss to actual hosting, without reducing it to issuing an invitation.

summary: Maintain the inherited III maʕəzle/maʕəz allocation and cross-reference to ʕzz. The authorized lookups show ʕzz II mʕazazle and ʕzm II/III with a retained final m, so root merger or assumed m-loss is not demonstrated.
PrS 83/47–48 reverses host and guest. l-marked lu Saʕid and lu kurrəko identify the respective hosts; the overt zero-marked Saʕid in verse 48 is the guest.

Hospitality is sustained until evening at PrS 83/47. The widened gloss describes actual hosting; the inherited invitation clause may still involve ʕzm and remains flagged by its existing editorial note.
The current parsed Preterit contains one example with an attached Russian editorial note. The note is not a separate example and needs no invented structural correction.
Are these hospitality forms historically or synchronically ʕyz 2, ʕzz or an unusual ʕzm form? Collate the inherited Russian note before moving any example.
Confirm the implicit host switch at PrS 7/10; the German names Ḥetəm, while the Turoyo initially foregrounds the dervish.
